prompt:
Let $z=\dfrac{3+4i}{1-2i}$.

**(a)** Express $z$ in the form $a+bi$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find $|z|$ and write down $z^{*}$. **[2]**

**(c)** State the quadrant in which $z$ lies and hence explain why $\arg z\neq\arctan(-2)$. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator: $\dfrac{(3+4i)(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)}$ **(M1)** $=\dfrac{-5+10i}{5}$ **(A1)** $=-1+2i$ **(A1)**

**(b)** $|z|=\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt5$ **(A1)**; $z^{*}=-1-2i$ **(A1)**

**(c)** Real part negative, imaginary part positive: second quadrant. $\arctan(-2)$ lies in the fourth quadrant, so $\arg z=\pi-\arctan2\approx2.03$ **(R1)**.

Let $z=a+bi$: $(a+bi)+2(a-bi)=3a-bi$ **(M1)(A1)**

Equate real and imaginary parts: $3a=6$, $-b=-3$ **(M1)**, so $z=2+3i$ **(A1)**

Two complex numbers are equal only when both real parts and both imaginary parts are equal — one complex equation gives two real equations.

prompt:
Let $z=3+i$.

**(a)** Plot $z$, $z^{*}$ and $iz$ on an Argand diagram. **[2]**

**(b)** Describe the geometric transformation that maps $z$ to $iz$. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $z=(3,1)$, $z^{*}=(3,-1)$ (reflection in the real axis), $iz=3i+i^{2}=-1+3i$, i.e. $(-1,3)$ **(A2)**

**(b)** Rotation by $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ anticlockwise about the origin **(A1)** — multiplying by $i=\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi2$ adds $\frac\pi2$ to the argument and leaves the modulus unchanged.
